title: Theseus and the Minotaur
objective: After this level you can retell the myth of the Labyrinth.
summary: Theseus ended Minos’s tribute of young Athenians by killing the Minotaur, finding his way out with Ariadne’s thread, the clew that gave us the word clue.

cards.headline: Every time you look for a clue, you’re following a Greek myth.
cards.body: The word began as a ball of thread in the Labyrinth on Crete. Here’s how it got there.

cards.headline: A terrible tribute
cards.body: Remember Level 3’s myth: King Minos kept the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in a Labyrinth built by Daedalus. To avenge his son Androgeos, killed by Athenians, Minos made Athens send seven youths and seven maidens to be devoured by it: every ninth year in one version, every year in another. Fourteen young Athenians, fed to a monster.

mascot.line: This is Level 3’s myth again: the King Minos that Evans named the Minoans after.

cards.headline: Theseus volunteers
cards.body: When the third tribute came due, Theseus volunteered to go. He was the son of King Aegeus of Athens (or, in another version, of Poseidon). On Crete, Minos’s own daughter, Ariadne, helped him: with her thread, he found his way back out of the Labyrinth after killing the Minotaur. The enemy king’s daughter handed the hero the way home.

cards.fact: The English word “clue” comes from “clew”, a ball of thread.
cards.context: Its meaning shifted because of the clew Ariadne gave Theseus to guide him out of the Labyrinth. The spelling “clue” appears by the mid-1400s, and by the 1620s a clue could be anything that points the way, maze or no maze. Every detective story owes Ariadne a thank-you note.

cards.headline: The wrong sail
cards.body: Theseus had promised his father a signal: if he survived, his ship would come home under a white sail instead of the usual black one. He forgot. Seeing the black sail, Aegeus believed his son was dead and killed himself; in one version he drowned himself in the sea, which was called the Aegean ever after. The hero won, and his father never knew.

cards.headline: The Labyrinth: solved
learned: Athens sent seven youths and seven maidens
Clue comes from clew, a ball of thread
The forgotten sail cost Aegeus his life

questions.prompt: What did King Minos force Athens to send to Crete?

options.label: A ship full of gold every year
Seven youths and seven maidens for the Minotaur
Its best builders to extend the Labyrinth
Prince Theseus as a royal hostage

questions.explanation: To avenge his son Androgeos, Minos made Athens send seven youths and seven maidens to be devoured by the Minotaur.

questions.prompt: How did Ariadne’s gift to Theseus give English the word “clue”?

options.label: Clue was Ariadne’s name in Greek
Theseus wrote the word on the Labyrinth walls
options.rationale: The word is English, from clew.

options.label: Her clew guided him out, so the word came to mean a guide
Minos used the word for his tribute ships
options.rationale: It comes from a ball of thread.

questions.explanation: Clue comes from clew, a ball of thread; because Ariadne’s clew led Theseus out, it came to mean anything that points the way.

questions.prompt: Level 3’s Arthur Evans dug up a palace at Knossos. Why did some link it to the Labyrinth of Theseus’s myth?

options.label: He found the Minotaur’s bones there
A Linear A tablet there named Theseus
options.rationale: Linear A has never been deciphered.

options.label: It held a statue of Ariadne with a thread
options.rationale: The link was the building’s layout.

options.label: Its twisting maze of rooms and corridors

questions.explanation: The palace’s maze of rooms and corridors, right where the myth put the maze, led some archaeologists to link it with the Labyrinth.
